**Verdict:** No, not as a full startup while you're still a student. Paul Graham would tell you to keep going on the side project, and to run with it only if it starts to take off on its own.

**Based on:** said it (the question is directly addressed, in 2014 and again in 2026)

**Why they'd say it**
- Founding a startup and being a student don't mix: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]; https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)
- Don't do it at 20: "Do not start a startup in college." "20 is not the optimal time to do it." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 18:56; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s)
- Waiting costs you nothing: "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s)
- The exception is a project that takes off by itself: "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s). He cites Facebook as the example.
- Projects are the best way to learn, and he wants students to have room for them: "Projects are the best source of knowledge, the best source of founding teams, and the best source of startup ideas." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]; https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)
- Learning by doing still applies: "if you're merely unsure of whether you're gonna be able to do it, the only way to find out is to try, just not now." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 23:58; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1438s)

**How the advice has shifted:** In 2014 he told students to wait. In a 2026 essay to universities, he argues for giving students free time so side projects can turn into startups. He still says a startup and full-time study don't mix, and that a project which takes off forces a choice: "Are the students just supposed to abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]). This is a shift in emphasis, not a reversal. ([[tensions]])

**What would change their answer:** If your side project is taking off on its own, like Facebook did, he'd say it may be reasonable to run with it. He doesn't say whether that means dropping out, only that you'd have to choose. Note too that the 2026 essay is addressed to universities, not students, so it doesn't say outright what a student should do. The advice about college comes from YC's founder, who has a stake in the YC model ([[profile]]).

**Practical read for you:** keep building the side project, use the time you have, and put more weight on it if users are pulling it forward. The question he'd ask is whether people want it and whether it keeps growing, not whether you should quit now.

*Basis: the 2014 Stanford lecture (Lecture 3, "Before the Startup") and PG's 2026 essay "How Universities Should Prepare Founders." Both are cited in the vault's college leaf ([[founders/becoming-a-founder/should-i-start-a-startup-in-college]]).*

**Verdict:** Yes, at least for a while. Paul Graham says you should go to Silicon Valley, but he means a stint, not a permanent move: "You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go."

**Based on:** said it. He addressed this exact situation in a talk he gave in Stockholm (April 2026).

**Why he'd say it**
- **Peers:** "You get the best peers. The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 1:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s)
- **Serendipity:** "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 3:20, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s)
- **Pace and confidence:** "Things also tend to move faster in the big centers because the people are better, they're more confident, and that's more decisive." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 3:53, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=233s)
- **The biggest effect is on you:** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 8:19, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s) Seeing big fish up close turns an impossible goal into a hard but definite one.

**What he says about Stockholm specifically**
- He argues that founders who go and come back are one of the best ways to make Stockholm a startup hub: "as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 16:10, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=970s) ([[startups/location/building-a-startup-hub-outside-the-valley]])
- He says a hub needs only "a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them." ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 21:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1269s)

**What would change his answer / caveats**
- **Conflict of interest:** He says so himself: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point" ([[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]] @ 17:16). He recommends doing YC as the way to go, and YC makes money from founders who come.
- **Weak data:** He says YC startups that go home are "only about half as likely to become unicorns," but he also says this is mostly selection bias, since confident founders may be the ones who stay. No numbers or method are shown.
- **Softer later view:** Sam Altman (July 2026) agrees that moving to the Bay Area was the best way to find co-founders, but says he has "less of an intuition for it now" and is less sure it holds for the next ten years ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]]). See [[startups/location/should-you-move-to-silicon-valley]].
- **Not in the vault:** The vault doesn't know your stage, team or whether you have co-founders in Stockholm. PG's "go for a bit, then come back" answer is the part that applies to you. Whether it's worth the cost depends on facts about your situation that the vault can't see.

**My read:** PG wouldn't say you need to move for good. He'd say go for a while, build a network and see how the best startups work, then come back, ideally through YC.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop treating the pitch as the job. Spend the time building something customers use and growing it, so investors come to you. Months of pitching with no close is a waste, and the time should go into the company.

**Based on:** said it. Seibel addressed fundraising directly in the October 2026 "Dalton + Michael" episode.

**Why he'd say it**
- On the wasted time: "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a it's like a drag on the industry." He calls it that from his own experience at Justin.tv, where he spent about eight months trying to raise ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 6:44, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s).
- On the deck: "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 10:03, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s)
- On the pitch itself: when Socialcam was the number two app in the App Store, "one of our pitch decks kind of just was like here's some questions you can ask us." He says the deck barely mattered then ([[yt-7TU636F_yVQ]] @ 9:30, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s).
- Investors told him they chase 80–90% of their deals rather than getting through the front door, so the goal is to become a company they chase ([[fundraising/investors/how-to-convince-investors]]).
- Seibel's Justin.tv story has the same shape. After about eight months of failing to raise, with two months of runway left, the team went for profitability, and he says they got more done in those two months than in the months of pitching ([[fundraising/investors/why-investors-string-founders-along]]).

**How this maps to your situation**
Months of follow-ups with no close is the pattern he calls a drag. Each meeting is a deck review, not progress on the company. His test is whether the investors you're meeting would chase you, and if they wouldn't, more polishing won't change that. The question to ask is what traction would make them come to you.

**What would change his answer**
- If your company is already growing and investors are pushing for terms, the calculation shifts. He doesn't say to stop raising while you're getting close.
- His own view is tied to a specific period. The Justin.tv story is an example of a company that was not fundable and got through by becoming profitable.

**Caveats**
- Caldwell co-hosts the episode and is a partner at Standard Capital, the show's sponsor. Their advice to respect founders' time comes from an active investor whose fund holds up its own process as the model ([[profile]]). Discount that somewhat.
- PG's 2014 view points the same way: fundraising tricks matter far less than a product users love ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 13:17). That gives independent support for the principle, though the advice on time limits comes only from the investor side.

**Verdict:** Stop paying lawyers to fight over stock that Seibel would say is worth almost nothing before product-market fit. Settle fast, with no fault on either side, a small stake for the leaver, reasonable severance, and clean paperwork. Then put the time into the decision that matters more: whether to keep going.

**Based on:** follows from what they said (confidence: medium-high). Seibel has a direct rule for breakups where the stock is worth nothing, and Caldwell adds the no-fault framing. Neither addressed a case quite like yours, where the company is "clearly over" and one founder is holding on to vested stock.

**How we get there**
1. The nearest case is a co-founder breakup before product-market fit. Seibel: "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 11:36; [[hiring/cofounders/handling-a-cofounder-breakup]])
2. His rules for the stake and the process: "After a number of years, 5% typical. Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." and "Do reasonable severance, sign clean paperwork and and peace out." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 21:22, 18:39; [[thinking/seibel]])
3. Your case falls under that rule, because he sets the stake by when the person leaves, not by what they've vested. He says a departing founder should give back most of their stock "even if vested," because "the vast majority of the value this company could create hasn't been created yet." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 14:47; [[hiring/cofounders/splitting-equity-when-a-cofounder-leaves]])

**Why they'd say it**
- Lawyers are the main risk, not the stock: "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 12:07)
- Don't make a third party the judge: "If you're using someone to mediate this, don't make them the judge." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 19:46)
- Caldwell's version: "Don't try to ruin the other person." and "being known as the super litigious scorched earth person, you're never going to work again." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 13:42, 16:28; [[hiring/cofounders/handling-a-cofounder-breakup]])
- On the decision itself: "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 9:26)

**What would change their answer**
- **Misconduct.** Seibel: "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." This advice is only for a no-fault split.
- **The company continues.** If you keep building, the advice favors whoever stays, since the value is still ahead. If you shut down, the stock is worth close to nothing and the fight is mostly about ego.
- **Whose side you're on.** Seibel's stance is that the founder who stays should be generous, not the one who leaves. If you're the one staying, that's your rule; if you're the one leaving, it's his rule applied to you.

**Caveats**
- The vault has no guidance on vested-stock mechanics, tax, or what your lawyers' letters actually say. The equity percentages are rules of thumb, and Seibel gives them inconsistently: "under 2%" at 18:39, "1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%" at 21:22.
- Seibel's breakup advice comes from episodes sponsored by Standard Capital, the fund Caldwell co-founded. That interest is in keeping equity with the company's future, so it's not neutral. The vault flags this in [[profile]].
- Nothing here is legal advice. Your lawyers should handle the paperwork. The point from Seibel is to stop letting them run the negotiation.

**Premise correction:** Garry Tan didn't say this. Sam Altman did, in the closing conversation at Startup School 2026, with Tan as the host. Altman is a former YC president and OpenAI's CEO.

**Verdict:** Altman's reason is network effects. Being in the Bay Area with YC puts you around the people you'll co-found with, and he says the advantage has grown: "the distance between like YC and second place has expanded."

**Based on:** said it (Altman, at 16:56 of [the Startup School talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s), [[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]]). He gives no numbers for the gap.

**Why he says it**
- Five or ten years ago, the main limit on how many good startups YC could fund was co-founder matching: "a lot of really talented people… just couldn't find their tribe" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:25).
- Moving to the Bay Area was the best way to find your people, and "you just like magic happened," through lucky chances and collisions ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56).
- "This is a reminder of the power of network effects." He follows with advice to find networks that help you meet future co-founders, citing his own OpenAI co-founders, whom he met years earlier ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 17:28).

**How much weight to give it:** He flags the conflict himself: "I can say this, Gary probably can't." That is, Tan, as YC's head, couldn't say it without seeming self-interested. Altman's own position is a stake too. He's a former YC president and runs OpenAI, a YC alumni company. The claim is also a story from one winner's hindsight, and the vault has no data on YC's share of founders or on the gap versus other accelerators ([[hiring/cofounders/finding-cofounders-and-your-people]]).

**What would change his view:** He suggests the premium depends on the network effects of being in the Valley. If remote founding or other hubs matched the Bay Area's density of co-founder matching, the premium he describes would shrink. PG argues the opposite, that Stockholm-style hubs can work with critical mass ([[startups/location/building-a-startup-hub-outside-the-valley]]). Tan has no comparable statement in the vault.

**Verdict:** The vault doesn't support the premise. I found no statement where Livingston says early YC backed aggressive or ruthless founders because they win. Her documented view is close to the opposite: she funded earnest people, screened out conceited applicants, and judged founders on character and their co-founder relationship.

**Based on:** said it (for the correction). She never said the claim, and the vault doesn't show her believing it.

**What the vault shows instead**
- She judged founders on whether they "seem earnest," "determined," and "flexible minded," and above all on "the relationship between the co-founders" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s).
- "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51).
- She declined applicants she judged conceited, and says that shaped the alumni culture: "early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 15:27; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=927s).
- In a later talk she says founders need "a certain amount of boldness" to work on ideas others call stupid, and must keep going through rejection ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 25:45). That's the closest thing to "aggressive," and it's about persistence, not ruthlessness.

**Where "ruthless" does appear**
The only raw hit is about investors, not founders, and she sets herself against it. "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless - for a couple of them that I know I cared about how founders were feeling" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 17:44; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s). She describes YC as "a family" with her as its "mom," and says she counseled founders through overwhelm and co-founder breakups.

**What would change this:** a transcript or source where she explicitly praises ruthlessness in founders. The vault has none. If you have a specific source in mind, I can check it. Adding it to the vault would require a fetch and compile first.
